items.q: orders.customer_id REFERENCES customers(id) with no ON DELETE clause. Customer 7 has 3 orders. What happens on DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 7?
options: The customer and the 3 orders are deleted
The delete fails with a foreign key violation
The customer is deleted and the orders get customer_id NULL
The delete succeeds and the orders keep customer_id 7
items.explain: The default action is NO ACTION / RESTRICT, so a parent row with children cannot be removed; ON DELETE CASCADE or SET NULL would change that.

items.q:
This query on a 5-million-row table takes 4 seconds. EXPLAIN shows "Seq Scan on orders". Which change most likely fixes it?

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1234;
items.explain: A B-tree index on the filtered column lets the planner use an Index Scan instead of reading every row.

items.q: A students table stores hobbies as a comma-separated text column "cricket,chess,music". What is the standard schema fix?
options: A separate student_hobbies table with (student_id, hobby) rows
Store the list as an integer code
items.explain: One value per cell (first normal form) makes hobbies searchable, countable and joinable; a child table models a one-to-many relation.

items.q: Session A runs BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 1; and has not committed. Session B runs SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id = 1; at the default isolation level. What does B see?
items.explain: Postgres uses MVCC; under READ COMMITTED a plain SELECT reads the last committed version and does not block on writers.

items.q: Which column type is the right choice for storing ₹ amounts like 1,25,000.50 in an invoices table?
items.explain: NUMERIC stores exact decimals; floating types round in binary and cause paise errors when totals are summed.

items.q:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints:

Index Scan using idx_email on users
  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=80)
  (actual time=0.031..0.033 rows=1 loops=1)

Which statement is true?
options: Estimated 1 row, got 1 row, via the index
The index was skipped because cost is low
items.explain: cost is a unitless estimate, actual time is in ms, rows shows estimate versus actual, and width is the average row size in bytes.

items.q: A migration adds NOT NULL to users.phone, but 200 existing rows have NULL phone. What happens when it runs?
options: Those rows get an empty string
The migration fails; you must backfill the values first
It succeeds and only new inserts are checked
items.explain: Constraints are checked against existing data when added, so you backfill (or add a DEFAULT) before tightening the column.

items.q: Why do teams use migration files (Alembic, Flyway, Liquibase) instead of changing tables by hand in the database?
options: Migrations run faster than ALTER TABLE
Schema changes are versioned and applied identically in every environment
Postgres does not allow manual ALTER TABLE
Migrations skip the need for backups
items.explain: A migration is code: it is reviewed, ordered and rerun on every environment, so schemas never drift between machines.

items.q: orders has millions of rows and a B-tree index on created_at. Which WHERE clause can actually use that index?
items.explain: Wrapping the column in a function hides it from a plain B-tree index; a range on the raw column keeps the index usable.

items.q: A transfer moves ₹1,000 from account 1 to account 2. Which sequence is correct so that a crash never leaves money missing?
options: UPDATE debit; COMMIT; UPDATE credit; COMMIT;
BEGIN; UPDATE debit; UPDATE credit; COMMIT;
UPDATE debit; UPDATE credit; (autocommit handles it)
BEGIN; UPDATE debit; COMMIT; UPDATE credit;
items.explain: Both updates inside one transaction are atomic: either both are committed or, on failure, both are rolled back.

items.q: enrollments(student_id, course_id, joined_on). A student must not enrol in the same course twice, but may take many courses. Which key definition enforces this?
items.explain: A composite key on the pair allows many rows per student and per course but rejects a repeated (student, course) combination.
